titleBlock.heading: UNIT 16: REFRACTION THROUGH PRISMS   Content Area: Waves & Optics
titleBlock.subtitle: All-possible NEB questions  •  short precise answers  •  exam shortcuts  •  worked examples

questions.question: Q1. Define the angle of minimum deviation of a prism.
questions.answer: It is the smallest possible deviation of the central ray for a given prism, occurring when the ray passes symmetrically (angle of incidence = angle of emergence) and the ray lies parallel to the base inside the prism.
questions.shortcut: δ_min when i₁ = i₂ and ray ∥ base.
questions.example: At δ_min the refraction is symmetric.

questions.question: Q2. Derive the refractive index from minimum deviation: n = sin[(A+δ_m)/2] / sin(A/2).
questions.answer: At δ_min, i₁ = i₂ = i and r₁ = r₂ = A/2. From i = (δ_m + A)/2, applying Snell's law n = sin i / sin r gives n = sin[(A+δ_m)/2]/sin(A/2).

questions.question: Q3. A prism of A = 60° has minimum deviation δ_m = 40°. Find its refractive index.
Q4. Explain a prism spectroscope briefly.
questions.answer: White light passing through a prism disperses into its colors (refractive index depends on wavelength). A telescope with a scale at the minimum-deviation position lets one measure n for each spectral line and hence identify wavelengths.
questions.shortcut: Prism + telescope + spectral scale; dispersion separates colors.
questions.example: A prism separates white light into a rainbow band.

questions.question: Q5. Find the angle of deviation of a prism A = 60° with n = 1.5 for a ray passing at minimum deviation.
questions.answer: At minimum deviation n = sin[(A+δ)/2]/sin(A/2) → sin[(60+δ)/2] = 1.5×sin30 = 0.75 → (60+δ)/2 = 48.6° → δ ≈ 37°. ▥ 16.1–16.2 Minimum Deviation & Refractive Index  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Minimum Deviation in a Prism (what it gives) ▣ 16.3 Small-Angle Prism Deviation & Dispersion

questions.question: Q6. Show that for a small-angle prism, δ = (n−1)A.
questions.answer: For A small (in radians), the deviation δ = i₁ + i₂ − A. At minimum deviation and small angles, i₂ ≈ (n−1)A/2 and i₁ ≈ (n−1)A/2, so δ = (n−1)A.

questions.question: Q7. Explain dispersive power of a prism and its dependence.
questions.answer: Dispersive power ω = (δ_v − δ_r)/δ, the ratio of the violet deviation to the mean deviation. It measures how well the prism separates colors and is larger for the crown/glass prism with high ω (flint glass has higher ω than crown glass).
questions.example: Flint glass splits colors more (bigger ω).

questions.question: Q8. State achromatism and its application.
questions.answer: Achromatism means correcting chromatic aberration by combining prisms/lenses so that two colors have the same net effect: (n_F−1)A + (n_C−1)A' = 0 while still dispersing. This is the principle of an achromatic doublet lens.
questions.shortcut: Combine two prisms; net deviation zero, dispersion not.
questions.example: Achromatic lenses combine crown + flint glass.

questions.question: Q9. Find the deviation of a 1° prism with n = 1.61.
Q10. Why does violet bend more than red in a prism?
questions.answer: Refractive index decreases with increasing wavelength (n_blue > n_red), so shorter (violet) wavelengths have a larger index and a larger deviation. This is dispersion; the violet edge is always more refracted. ▥ 16.3 Small-Angle Prism Deviation & Dispersion  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Dispersion vs Deviation PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
questions.shortcut: n decreases as λ increases → violet bends most.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T1. Derive the refractive index of a prism at minimum deviation: n = sin[(A+δ_m)/2]/sin(A/2).
theoryItems.answer: At δ_min, i = (δ_m + A)/2 and r = A/2. Applying Snell's law n = sin i / sin r gives n = sin[(A+δ_m)/2]/sin(A/2). Measuring A and δ_m yields n.

theoryItems.question: [State] T2. State the minimum-deviation condition for a prism.
theoryItems.answer: At minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically: angle of incidence = angle of emergence (i₁ = i₂), and the refracted ray lies parallel to the base. Then i = (δ_m + A)/2 and r = A/2.
theoryItems.shortcut: At δ_min: i₁ = i₂, ray ∥ base.

theoryItems.question: [Compare] T3. Compare a prism and a diffraction grating as dispersive elements.
theoryItems.answer: A prism disperses by wavelength-dependent refractive index (dispersion varies nonlinearly with λ, poor at short wavelengths). A grating disperses by interference (angular separation linear in λ, works over a wide range and gives multiple orders). Gratings give higher dispersion but prisms are continuous and simpler.
theoryItems.shortcut: Prism: n(λ) dispersion; Grating: interference, linear in λ.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T4. Explain deviation in a small-angle prism and its use in a spectroscope.
theoryItems.answer: For small angles, the deviation of a thin prism is δ = (n−1)A (in radians), independent of the incident angle; this simple, proportional deviation is used in a small-angle prism spectroscope (or in the Fritsch/Abbe setups) to spread colors in a compact instrument.
theoryItems.example: Thin prisms are used in prism-spectroscopes and in laser alignment.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T5. Explain the prism spectroscope and how wavelengths are identified.
theoryItems.answer: White light through a slit is dispersed by a prism into a spectrum; a telescope with a scale at the eyepiece measures each spectral line's minimum deviation δ_m, from which n is computed and the wavelength identified against a reference.
theoryItems.shortcut: Slit + prism + telescope + scale; measure δ_m per color.
theoryItems.example: Each line's δ_m gives its n and hence λ.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain dispersive power of a prism and its significance.
theoryItems.answer: Dispersive power ω = (δ_v − δ_r)/δ_m, the ratio of the violet–red deviation to the mean deviation. It measures how well the prism separates colors and is larger for flint glass than for crown glass, so a flint prism gives more color spread.
theoryItems.example: Flint glass splits colors more than crown glass.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain the Achromatic condition for two prisms.
theoryItems.answer: Two prisms (of different materials) are in opposition so that the net deviation for two colors is zero while the net dispersion remains: (n_F−1)A + (n_C−1)A′ = 0, or (ωA+ω′A′)=0. This produces a 'deviation without dispersion' (achromatism), the idea later adapted to an achromatic doublet lens.
theoryItems.example: Used in an achromatic doublet lens.

theoryItems.question: [Why] T8. Why does a prism split white light into a spectrum (why does violet bend most)?
theoryItems.answer: The refractive index decreases with increasing wavelength (n_violet > n_red), so shorter wavelengths are refracted more; violet therefore bends most and red the least, separating the white into a fan of colors. This is the basis of all prism dispersion.
theoryItems.shortcut: n decreases with λ → violet most bent.

[Numerical] T10. A thin (small-angle) prism has A = 1° and n = 1.61. Find its deviation.

▣ 16.1–16.2 Minimum Deviation & Refractive Index
Q1. Define the angle of minimum deviation of a prism.

Answer:  It is the smallest possible deviation of the central ray for a given prism, occurring when the ray passes symmetrically (angle of incidence = angle of emergence) and the ray lies parallel to the base inside the prism.
⚡ Shortcut:  δ_min when i₁ = i₂ and ray ∥ base.
Example:  At δ_min the refraction is symmetric.
Q2. Derive the refractive index from minimum deviation: n = sin[(A+δ_m)/2] / sin(A/2).
Answer:  At δ_min, i₁ = i₂ = i and r₁ = r₂ = A/2. From i = (δ_m + A)/2, applying Snell's law n = sin i / sin r gives n = sin[(A+δ_m)/2]/sin(A/2).
⚡ Shortcut:  n = sin[(A+δ_m)/2]/sin(A/2).
Example:  Measure A and δ_m → n.
Q3. A prism of A = 60° has minimum deviation δ_m = 40°. Find its refractive index.
⚡ Shortcut:  n = sin[(A+δ)/2]/sin(A/2).
Example:  ≈ 1.53.
Q4. Explain a prism spectroscope briefly.

Answer:  White light passing through a prism disperses into its colors (refractive index depends on wavelength). A telescope with a scale at the minimum-deviation position lets one measure n for each spectral line and hence identify wavelengths.
⚡ Shortcut:  Prism + telescope + spectral scale; dispersion separates colors.
Example:  A prism separates white light into a rainbow band.
Q5. Find the angle of deviation of a prism A = 60° with n = 1.5 for a ray passing at minimum deviation.
Answer:  At minimum deviation n = sin[(A+δ)/2]/sin(A/2) → sin[(60+δ)/2] = 1.5×sin30 = 0.75 → (60+δ)/2 = 48.6° → δ ≈ 37°.
⚡ Shortcut:  Use δ_m: sin[(A+δ)/2] = n·sin(A/2).
Example:  ≈ 37° minimum deviation.

▣ 16.3 Small-Angle Prism Deviation & Dispersion
Q6. Show that for a small-angle prism, δ = (n−1)A.
Answer:  For A small (in radians), the deviation δ = i₁ + i₂ − A. At minimum deviation and small angles, i₂ ≈ (n−1)A/2 and i₁ ≈ (n−1)A/2, so δ = (n−1)A.
⚡ Shortcut:  δ = (n−1)A (radians).
Example:  A 2° prism, n=1.5 → δ = 1°.
Q7. Explain dispersive power of a prism and its dependence.

Answer:  Dispersive power ω = (δ_v − δ_r)/δ, the ratio of the violet deviation to the mean deviation. It measures how well the prism separates colors and is larger for the crown/glass prism with high ω (flint glass has higher ω than crown glass).
⚡ Shortcut:  ω = (δ_v−δ_r)/δ; flint > crown.
Example:  Flint glass splits colors more (bigger ω).
Q8. State achromatism and its application.

Answer:  Achromatism means correcting chromatic aberration by combining prisms/lenses so that two colors have the same net effect: (n_F−1)A + (n_C−1)A' = 0 while still dispersing. This is the principle of an achromatic doublet lens.
⚡ Shortcut:  Combine two prisms; net deviation zero, dispersion not.
Example:  Achromatic lenses combine crown + flint glass.
Q9. Find the deviation of a 1° prism with n = 1.61.
⚡ Shortcut:  δ = (n−1)A.
Example:  ≈ 0.61°.
Q10. Why does violet bend more than red in a prism?

Answer:  Refractive index decreases with increasing wavelength (n_blue > n_red), so shorter (violet) wavelengths have a larger index and a larger deviation. This is dispersion; the violet edge is always more refracted.
⚡ Shortcut:  n decreases as λ increases → violet bends most.
Example:  Rainbow: violet inside, red outside.
